vignette:
He can still feel the weight of his father's hand. Not the slap itself-that part is a blur of sound and heat-but the pause before it, the way the whole kitchen would go silent, the refrigerator humming as if it were listening. He was six, maybe seven, standing at the table with a glass of milk he'd spilled. His father's shadow fell across the linoleum first, then the hand. After that, he learned to watch shadows.

Now, at sixty-six, he spends his days watching code. He is a software engineer for a mid-sized firm, and his colleagues describe him as "meticulous," "unflappable," "the guy who catches the edge cases no one else sees." He does catch them-but not because he's gifted. Because he learned early that missing a detail meant pain. A misplaced semicolon in a deployment script once cost him a sleepless weekend, not because the bug was hard to fix, but because the knot in his stomach wouldn't let him rest until every line was clean. He runs the test suite three times before he can push to production. He checks his work, then checks it again, then checks the logs for errors he already knows aren't there.

His wife, Nora, knows parts of the story. She knows he flinches when she comes up behind him too quickly, and that he never lets anyone stand between him and the door in a restaurant. She knows he sleeps with his back to the wall. But she does not know that every time he hears a loud noise-a car backfiring, a dropped pan in the kitchen-his body remembers the crack of a belt buckle against a wooden chair. He does not tell her because telling would mean reliving, and he has spent fifty years not reliving.

The memories come anyway. Not as clear scenes, but as sensations: the smell of coffee and sweat, the cold sting of a leather belt left coiled on the bathroom sink. He will be writing a function, his mind perfectly focused on a loop of integers, and then suddenly his jaw is tight and his palms are damp. He doesn't know why. He looks at the clock and realizes he has been staring at the same line of code for ten minutes. The feeling passes, but the afternoon is ruined. He blames it on aging, on too much caffeine.

He avoids his father's side of the family entirely. He did not attend the funeral four years ago-he had a "conflict," a project launch, though the launch was two weeks later. His sister still sends Christmas cards, but he does not open them. He keeps a flat, professional tone with everyone, including his own children. They love him, he knows, but he cannot quite feel the warmth of it. There is a pane of glass between him and most of the world. When his grandson was born, he felt a flicker of something-maybe joy-but it was so brief and so thin that by the time he tried to hold onto it, it was gone.

At night, he lies awake beside Nora, listening. The house settles, the furnace clicks on. He catalogues every sound: a creak that could be footsteps, a rattle that could be a hand on a doorknob. He knows it is irrational. The man who hurt him has been dead for years. But the body does not believe in timelines. It waits. It listens. And when sleep finally comes, it is shallow and filled with rooms he does not want to enter.

He has never asked for help. He tells himself he is fine-he is functional, successful, married. He keeps his life small and orderly, and that works. Most days, the shadow is just a shadow. But sometimes, in the quiet of late afternoon, when the code compiles clean on the first try and there is nothing left to double-check, he sits very still, and he wonders why he still feels like he is holding his breath.
